catalog_quote: To date, no prosodic phenomenon has come to light which would be strongly suggestive of lexical accent, but this is an issue which needs further research. Among other things, it will be necessary to have a closer look at how Waima’a accommodates the different accentual patterns occurring on Portuguese loanwords, which make up a substantial part of the Waima’a lexicon. ... 7 Conclusion. While still preliminary and incomplete, the analysis sketched in the preceding sections suggests that the Waima’a prosodic system is characterised by the following three core characteristics: 1. It has no lexical tone. 2. It has no lexical accent and hence also no intonational pitch accent.15 3. Intonation units are primarily characterised by a phrase accent on the penultimate syllable and a phrase-final boundary tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Himmelmann there is no word-level stress (lexical accent) and no lexical tone in Waima'a. The only regular prominence is a phrase accent on the penultimate syllable of the intonation unit (IU), followed by a boundary tone (H-L% declarative, H-H%, L-H% etc.). Words spoken in isolation therefore sound penult-stressed (e.g. ria-kuko 'nighttime', basara 'market', Figs. 20-22, pp. 64-65), but the same word inside an IU shows flat pitch with no prominent syllable (Fig. 23, p. 65), and any syllable, including the penult, can be reduced or omitted (p. 64), so the isolation prominence is attributed to utterance-level intonation, not lexical stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; no word-level stress is posited at all.
new_statements.exceptions: When the IU-final word is monosyllabic (e.g. allative particle di, or a VV sequence realised as a single long vowel), phrase accent and boundary tone both fall on the final syllable (pp. 53-54, 65). Himmelmann flags the accentual patterns of Portuguese loanwords, 'which make up a substantial part of the Waima'a lexicon', as unresolved (p. 66), and states that the analysis is preliminary and that words could alternatively carry a lexical accent that is 'ignored' by intonation (p. 63).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the intonation unit (phrase), not the word; citation forms in isolation show a penultimate H- rise which the author analyses as the unmarked declarative H-L% pattern (pp. 64-65). Data: ~1150 plotted utterances from elicited mini-discourses (14 speakers), word lists (2 speakers) and ~150 IUs of spontaneous DoBeS corpus speech (p. 49).
new_statements.identity_note: Himmelmann 2010 (p. 47) describes "the variety of Waima'a spoken in the village of Caisido and parts of the neighboring town of Baucau" (DoBeS Waima'a documentation corpus, main speaker Mauricio Belo). Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect glottocodes under waim1252; the language is also called Waimaha (Hull 2002) and Waimoa (Hajek & Bowden 2002).

(pp. 63-66) and sec. 7 (p. 66): no lexical tone, no lexical accent (word stress), no pitch accent; IUs have a phrase accent on the penultimate syllable plus a final boundary tone; isolation forms only look penult-stressed because of utterance intonation; Portuguese loans unresolved.

sources.note: Abstract (p. 347): many languages of the area 'appear to lack lexical stress as well as lexical tone'; p. 353: Waima'a listed with French and Indonesian as lacking lexical tone and postlexical pitch accents; p. 354: phrase accent 'mostly penultimate syllable, but sometimes also on ultima (e.g. Manado and Papuan Malay, Waima'a)'. Survey restating Himmelmann 2010.

sources.citation: Ewing, Michael C. & Marian Klamer. 2010. The languages of East Nusantara: an introduction. In Ewing & Klamer (eds.), East Nusantara (PL 618), 1-24 (p. 14).
sources.note: Editors' summary (p. 14): Waima'a 'appears to lack lexical accents' as well as accentual tone; contrasts with Tadmor's claim that East Nusantara languages 'often have regular penultimate lexical accents'. Second-hand, derived from Himmelmann's chapter.
